lines.text: song. It is unquestionable, and particularly so for Christians,
that the sensitive feeling for the splendours and the abundant
vitalities of nature is a feeling which conceals the sense of
God's presence and working, that the astonished delight in
the secret powers of nature really expresses our wonder at
the power and glory of God, and that the thankful exultation
in nature which rings out in poetry and song is at bottom
praise of God the Creator. Hence it is not surprising that
when such joy and gratitude are expressed in poetry, the
poem also speaks of God. So it is in the austere Pilgrim's Song
of Eichendorff: "When God wishes to bestow on you great
favour"
••. and concluding thus: "I accept in simple faith
the wise ruling of the good God; He who wills to maintain
the streams, the larks, the woods and the fields, has also
guided my life for the best." So it is too in the spring song of
Goethe, Ganymede, which to many of us is so attractive in the
musical setting of Schubert. The poem is penetrated with
love and yearning directed to the "all-loving Father":
"Beloved spring, how you encircle me with your flame in
the bright radiance of morning. O infinite beauty, with the
manifold raptures of love the holy feeling of your everlasting
warmth and glow pierces my heart." And so it goes on to the
conclusion:
"Upwards, upwards soars my heart, while the hovering
clouds sink down to meet the yearnings of love. To me they
incline! Upwards I rise to their bosom! I return the embrace
of love! Upwards I soar to your breast, O all-loving Father!"
Who would wish to deny that in such and countless similar
songs the voice of genuine religious feeling is heard, and that
the poet is feeling after God to find Him? And as Christians
should we wish to deny that poetry of this kind redounds to
the glory of the God whom we know as our Father in Jesus
Christ our Lord? It would be appropriate to quote in this
connexion what God declares through the prophet Malachi
to those priests of Jerusalem who consider that their sacrifices
are alone well-pleasing to Him:
